newsitem.title: FRANCE: French carmaker seeks longer barriers against Japan.
newsitem.headline: French carmaker seeks longer barriers against Japan.

text.p: Leading French carmaker Jacques Calvet on Wednesday said he wanted quotas limiting Japanese car imports into Europe extended beyond the year 2000, putting him at odds with the European carmakers association which he heads.
Calvet, chairman of PSA Peugeot Citroen, said Japanese carmakers have sold three million cars in Europe in excess of the quotas set in a 1991 Japanese-European accord.
"It'll be 3.6 million by the end of 1996 and the only way to absorb that surplus is to extend the accord," Calvet said.
The managing director of Toyota Motor Europe said he had no idea how Calvet came up with that figure.
"We have no idea how to respond to this claim. What I can say is that his claim is unfounded," Toyota managing director Tatsuo Takahashi told Reuters at the Paris car show.
"In the agreement between the Japanese government and the European Community about the importation of Japanese cars, to my understanding there is no specific calculation formula," he said.
Japanese cars now account for 11 percent of the annual European Union car sales of about 13 million.

Although Japanese sales have been below the actual quotas set in the accord for the past two years, the PSA group says a clause requires Japanese manufacturers to adapt their quota to market growth, which has been much weaker than anticipated since the 1993 European auto recession.
The European carmakers association ACEA has not taken an official stance, a spokesman said.
Industry sources say the sticking point is that the clause, included in an annex, is considered a "European understanding" that is not recognised by the Japanese.
"If the Japanese government doesn't know about it, then we don't," Haruyuki Miyadai, director of government relations at Toyota's European headquarters in Brussels, told Reuters.
Industry sources say Calvet does not have sufficient backing from European carmakers for his proposal, and any attempt to prolong the quota accord may run contrary to World Trade Organisation rules.
The twice yearly Japanese-European negotiations on imports are set to begin later this month.
Japanese carmakers have just under 11 percent of the western European market.
The ACEA members, who held a meeting on Wednesday, discussed a worry they all share -- the rapid inroads into their market by South Korean carmakers.

The Koreans' share of the market has jumped to 1.8 percent in August from less than 0.2 percent in 1990. By contrast, the share of the Korean market held by European carmakers has grown to 0.4 percent from 0.1 percent over the same period.
What alarms European carmakers most, Calvet said, were the Korean carmakers' ambitious production plans.
"Korean carmakers are seeking to develop not just their national market and reasonable exports, but to build a powerful base aimed at exports," he said.

He said Korean carmakers are aiming for production of 6.5 million cars by the year 2000, an amount equivalent to the entire Japanese market. But he declined to speculate on the source of financing for such a vast undertaking.
The ACEA has formed a working group to study the issue of Korean imports. Calvet said he hoped the group would shed more light on the situation "which is not altogether normal".
Industry sources say the Koreans and their relatively downscale car models may represent a bigger threat to European carmakers in the race to capture sales in emerging markets.
